why: In fraud, medical screening or churn, accuracy is misleading. A model that never flags fraud is 99% "accurate" and completely useless.
explain: The **confusion matrix** counts four outcomes: true positives (caught fraud), false positives (false alarms), false negatives (missed fraud) and true negatives.
**Precision** = of everything flagged, how much was really positive? It matters when false alarms are costly (blocking a genuine customer's card).
**Recall** = of all real positives, how many did we catch? It matters when misses are costly (missing a cancer).

**F1** balances the two. **ROC-AUC** measures ranking quality across all thresholds; **PR-AUC** is more informative when positives are rare. Most classifiers output probabilities; the **threshold** (default 0.5) is a business decision.

formula.plain: Precision: share of alarms that were real. Recall: share of real cases that raised an alarm.

example.title: Fraud model on 1,000 transactions (20 frauds)
steps: Model flags 30: 15 real frauds (TP), 15 false alarms (FP)
example.result: The useful story: "we catch 75% of fraud, and half of our alerts are real".

mistakes: Keeping the 0.5 threshold without checking business costs.
Reporting ROC-AUC alone for very rare events.
takeaways: Precision = trust in alarms; recall = coverage of real cases
Choose the threshold by the cost of errors

practice.code:
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, classification_report
y_true = [1]*20 + [0]*980
y_pred = [1]*15 + [0]*5 + [1]*15 + [0]*965
print(confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred))
print(classification_report(y_true, y_pred, digits=3))

check.q: Cancer screening: which metric matters most?
check.why: Missing a real case (false negative) is the costly error.
